an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics. Additionally, we touch on implications related to polyacetylene. While the material presented is primarily instructional, it does incorporate interactive elements and a glimpse at research involving interactions in extended topological systems. Specifically, we explore how multiple interacting electrons can stabilize a topological state even at finite doping levels. This is demonstrated through a numerical study using the time-dependent DFT and the vorticity analysis. Furthermore, we show that as the electron-electron interaction between adjacent electrons increases, the electron transport in these systems becomes less topologically secure, leading to a possible topological gap closure. This could provide insight into the effects of electron-electron interactions on the topological characteristics of 1D electronic structures. This material is intended to provide an educational foundation for understanding one-dimensional topological phases, interactions, and quantum electronics in general. While the talk mostly covers theoretical aspects, related experimental techniques and current research are briefly discussed. This is meant to provide an introductory foundation that can help readers navigate the growing body of one-dimensional topological phase research.

In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection. Consequently, this limits entanglement utilization in further quantum processing or applications. Fortunately, a new strategy has been proposed to create detection-free polarization entanglement between two photons. The method relies on type-II spontaneous parametric down-conversion and incorporates a walk-off process to postselection-free entangled states. This study develops a framework to assess policies based on welfare criteria that account for both subjective feelings and objective interests. We derive specific requirements for such a standard to produce the same prioritization of societal conditions as Pareto's unanimous principle. This approach can provide a more comprehensive understanding of social welfare, taking into account both the prioritization of individuals' personal desires and their broader, more tangible needs. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the importance of considering the way people's preferences are connected when designing a fair and representative social welfare order. Our findings are relevant to both the study of social choice and the development of policies that balance individual feelings and objective needs. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. A graph is perfect if every subset of vertices has a perfect matching. A graph is nearly perfect if for every pair of vertices, it either has a perfect matching or can be split into two disjoint paths. A graph has the NP-property if every pairing of K_G has a nearly perfect matching. A pairing Hamiltonian path (AHP) graph is one that possesses the PH-property, and this class includes bipartite double graphs and threshold graphs. A notable AHP graph with no perfect matching and having the largest possible order is the cube graph, which surpasses all other AHP graphs in order. Specifically, when a new edge is added, it follows the preferential attachment rule with a certain probability and otherwise forms between two randomly selected nodes.  This approach leads to a distribution of node in- and out-degrees that has less extreme outliers compared to a purely preferential attachment network, thereby improving upon this traditional model. This modification results in a network that exhibits a higher degree of heterogeneity with less extreme outliers. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. This study evaluates the performance of VSSA on an elastography phantom and compares its results with the established superposition of transmission and reception (STAR) technique. VSSA successfully estimates lateral displacement with a higher resolution and sampling frequency than its competitor, indicating its potential to contribute to the development of elastography and other applications utilizing high-resolution data. The novel VSSA technique exhibits promise for improving the lateral resolution and sampling frequencies of ultrasound data, thereby facilitating advancements in several ultrasound-based imaging techniques. Its implementation on a commercially available ultrasound system enables the technique to be readily integrated in clinical settings. Notably, VSSA's performance is unaffected by data sampling, thereby enabling the technique to be applied across various ultrasound systems with suitable beamforming capabilities.

Building on previous research by Eilers, Reutenauer, and Gastineau, who identified a criterion for two-sided recognizability, we derive a criterion for one-sided recognizability. This criterion demonstrates that any morphism composed of powers of letters can be made recognizable on one side if and only if a specific power of its associated C-matrix is recognizable on one side. Furthermore, we prove that the class of morphisms identifiable on one side is both closed under composition and category-wise transformations. Additionally, we prove that any morphism composed of powers of letters that is identifiable on one side can be broken down into a product of identifiable-on-one-side morphisms. Lastly, we show that identifying all square matrices recognizable on one side allows us to determine all morphisms identifiable on one side. This research provides a solution to an open question in the field. Moreover, we identify a necessary and sufficient condition for one-sided recognizability in terms of finite complete congruences generated by (extremely) weakly recognizable relations. This condition allows us to identify all fccs generating complete congruences that can lead to morphisms identifiable on one side. Finally, we list some specific powers of letters whose associated C-matrices are not identifiable on one side, demonstrating that our found criterion is both necessary and sufficient in this context. Building on past research, which suggested objectives such as minimum welfare and generalized Gini welfare for fair policies, we instead consider a fundamental approach. From an axiomatic standpoint, we identify four criteria for fair objectives and demonstrate that Nash social welfare uniquely satisfies these requirements, whereas previous proposals fail to meet all conditions. Next, we address the unknown model version of the problem by minimizing the difference in performance between fair policies optimized for minimum welfare, generalized Gini welfare, and Nash social welfare. Using optimistic planning, we propose a flexible learning algorithm and establish its performance limits relative to these three objectives. Additionally, we find that Nash social welfare regret experiences exponential growth with the number of agents, and demonstrate the potential for improvement in regret bounds by a factor of O(n) when focusing on minimum welfare objectives. All theoretical guarantees for our algorithm assume an assumption of exploratory preference variability, and without it, regret bounds would only improve by a factor of O(sqrt(n)) due to the inherent challenges in exploring the vast (n+1)-dimensional action space and state space. Experimental results substantiate the efficacy of our algorithm, and highlight the trade-offs between fairness objectives and regret performance. Ultimately, this research opens doors for designing fair policies with better performance and provides deeper insights into the trade-offs between different objectives. This involves translating base-type terms into multi-dimensional tuples of numbers, while higher-order terms are mapped to relationships between those tuples. The tuples used can convey type-related information; for instance, terms with a specific type may be associated with specific numerical values, like a pair representing execution time and memory consumption. When the gain is above a certain threshold, the computation of normal form proceeds as usual; otherwise, the search may be terminated to conserve resources. The metric is parameterizable, allowing one to balance the trade-off between the speed of computation and the comprehensiveness of the normal form. Resource Allocation (ONRA) plays a vital role in service provisioning. As a sequential problem with uncertain outcomes, it presents a suitable case for tackling via Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, current RL solutions face significant challenges stemming from high sample complexity requirements. To navigate this hurdle, training RL agents in isolation is impractical due to a lack of knowledge about future service demands, while online training in actual networks causes performance deterioration due to temporary sub-optimal policies during prolonged learning periods. This degradation is particularly pronounced in non-stationary ONRA scenarios, where adapting to shifting service requirements is crucial.
